about:

The shop focuses on custom handcrafted furniture, millwork, conference tables, and reception desks. Materials include solid wood, exotic veneers, high-end laminates, and real steel, combined with current manufacturing technology. Facility size, headcount, and annual volume are not published.

Clients span commercial, design, and hospitality sectors. Commercial accounts include American Airlines Center, AT&T Discovery District, and Marriott Hotels. Design-firm partners include Erin Sander Design, Marly & Co, SJL Design, Angeline Guido Design, and Autumn Cooper Design. Local hospitality projects include Lochlands Irish Pub in Lake Highlands, Revolving Kitchen in Fairview, Fortunate Sons in Garland, and Recess Dallas in Lakewood.

The company states that its innovative interpretation of residential and commercial furniture sets it apart, citing the use of premium materials and latest technology. It emphasizes fresh designs and fully customized solutions for conference rooms, lobby areas, reception desks, statement tables, and collaborative workspaces.

name: The Metal Guy LLC
old_description: Expert metal craftsmen with current experience in the marine trades work onsite at Safe Harbor Newport Shipyard. Welding and cutting machinery assure accurate fabrication and efficiency. Shipyard cranes provide the ability to move and manipulate massive plates and structures.
about:
The Metal Guy LLC operates onsite at Safe Harbor Newport Shipyard in Newport, Rhode Island. The limited‑liability company provides metal fabrication and repair services to the shipyard’s military and commercial clients. No founding year or ownership structure is disclosed in public materials; the business is identified by its trade name, TMG Newport, and a single point of contact, Kevin.

The shop specializes in marine alloys, working with aluminum, stainless steel, cupro‑nickel, duplex stainless, high‑nickel alloys, and bronze. Its craftsmen handle tubing, piping, and flat‑plate work both on board vessels and in the shop. Welding and cutting machinery support the fabrication process, while the shipyard’s cranes allow the team to move and position massive plates and structural assemblies.

Customers include military and commercial vessel owners, refit projects, and other onsite trades at the Newport Shipyard. The Metal Guy’s work spans new construction, repair, and refit scenarios where corrosion‑resistant alloys and precise fit‑up are required. The company does not publish a client list, but its location inside a full‑service shipyard places it alongside machine, electrical, and carpentry shops serving the same fleet.

The firm emphasizes its craftsmen’s current marine‑trades experience and breadth of alloy expertise as differentiators. Access to shipyard lifting equipment and the ability to work either dockside or in a controlled shop environment are cited as reasons customers engage TMG Newport for complex marine fabrication.

name: The Plastics Group of America
old_description: Offering custom compounding to meet customer’s needs since 1973
about:
The Plastics Group of America (TPG) is headquartered in Woonsocket, Rhode Island. The company traces its roots to 1973 when Bob Lebeaux founded Ralco Industries, Inc., a one-man operation buying and selling scrap plastics. In 1978 the firm added a grinder, baler, extruder and tractor‑trailer to enter recycling, and in 1980 began custom compounding reinforced thermoplastics under the Polifil® trade name. The business was renamed The Plastics Group of America in 1988, consolidating Ralco, Polifil® and the Transcontinental Polymers recycling unit. Today the company remains family‑led, with Lebeaux family members holding key executive and operational roles.

TPG operates more than 300,000 square feet of manufacturing space in Woonsocket, including the former Jules Desurmont Mill complex acquired in 2012. With a workforce of 60‑plus employees and annual revenue exceeding $50 million, the company custom‑compounds mineral‑ and glass‑filled polypropylene resins to precise mechanical, thermal and physical specifications. Its on‑site quality laboratory performs melt index, Izod, flexural, tensile, DSC, moisture, ash, Gardner impact and color testing on every batch. Beyond compounding, TPG provides recycling and toll‑processing services, color matching at no charge, and acts as a resin broker and distributor with stock ready for shipment.

The company serves processors in appliance, automotive, construction, consumer housewares, furniture, industrial/institutional/electronic, medical and personal care, packaging, and pump/pool/spa/irrigation markets. Customers include injection molders, extruders and blow‑molders who rely on TPG’s Polifil® resins for consistent performance in demanding applications.

TPG emphasizes its asset‑based manufacturing model, ISO 9001 certification and an on‑site testing lab as differentiators that enable tight lot‑to‑lot consistency whether the order is 100 pounds or one million pounds. The firm also highlights its recycling expertise, free color compounding, and a technical insights library that helps customers optimize molding processes.

name: The Tri-M Group, LLC
old_description: The Tri-M Group specializes in the design, installation and service of high voltage, electrical construction, building automation systems, data and telecommunications networks, security and energy analytics.
about:
The Tri-M Group, LLC was founded in 1964 by brothers Tom and Dick Musser in Kennett Square, Pennsylvania. Originally a small industrial and commercial electrical contractor, the company has grown to over 500 employees and operates from its headquarters in Kennett Square with additional offices in Lock Haven and Quakertown, Pennsylvania, Middletown, Delaware, and Baltimore, Maryland. In a move to preserve its independent culture and the legacy of founder Tom Musser, the company transitioned to 100% employee ownership through an Employee Stock Ownership Plan (ESOP).

The company provides design, installation, and ongoing service for critical infrastructure including high‑voltage electrical construction, building automation, data and telecommunications networks, security systems, and energy analytics. Its service portfolio covers 24/7 emergency and scheduled maintenance, preventative maintenance, panel fabrication, remote engineering, and hardware/software replacement. With a workforce exceeding 500, Tri‑M handles projects ranging from commercial buildings to industrial facilities across the Mid‑Atlantic region.

Tri‑M serves customers in energy analytics, building automation, security, network infrastructure, electrical construction, and high‑voltage sectors. Its client base includes commercial, industrial, and institutional facilities that require integrated critical‑infrastructure solutions, though specific customer names are not disclosed.

The company emphasizes its employee‑owned structure, a safety‑first culture, ethical decision‑making, collaborative problem‑solving, and a proprietary project‑navigation tool (ProNav) that lets customers track service requests and project progress in real time. A stated environmental goal aims to cut operational greenhouse‑gas emissions by roughly 10% by 2030.

The company distinguishes itself through its research-driven approach to historical accuracy, drawing on primary sources from the Victorian era, and by offering custom replication services that accommodate a range of input formats, from hand-drawn sketches to physical samples.

name: The Wooden Nickel - Custom Live Edge Furniture
old_description: Every once in a while a project comes through the shop that reminds us why we started building furniture in the first place. This past spring, a family from Marshall County asked for a live edge dining table big enough to hold three generations at once. They...
about:
The Wooden Nickel operates from Arab, Alabama, where it builds custom live‑edge furniture from locally sourced hardwood slabs. The company does not publish a founding year or ownership structure, but its blog posts describe a shop that began with a focus on honest craftsmanship — turning rough logs into dining tables, desks, and workstations meant to last generations.

Production centers on kiln‑dried slabs sourced from tree services and loggers. Each piece moves through stabilization, flattening, sanding, and, when needed, resin filling of cracks or knots before receiving multiple hand‑applied finish coats. Steel bases — ranging from simple dark‑finished legs to adjustable‑height desk frames made from high‑tolerance steel — are fitted in‑house. The shop handles one‑off commissions and larger custom runs alike, though it does not disclose facility size, headcount, or annual volume.

Customers span residential and commercial segments. A Marshall County family commissioned a three‑generation dining table; remote workers order wide slab workstations with cable management; local businesses have requested reinforced tables for offices, break rooms, and public areas that endure daily wear. The company notes that the same durability valued by commercial clients appeals to homeowners as well.

The Wooden Nickel positions itself against mass‑produced furniture, emphasizing “no templates, no shortcuts” and a slow, deliberate process — “if it wouldn’t hold up in our own homes, it doesn’t leave the shop.” The stated goal is furniture built for real life: sturdy, honest, and meant to outlast a warranty card.

The showroom presents two floors of Thos. Moser furniture designs alongside Maine artwork, with an attached carriage house serving as an outlet annex offering immediately available pieces. The facility provides scheduled consultations for both standard and custom furniture designs through the CIR program. Operating hours run Monday through Saturday 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. and Sunday noon to 5 p.m., with holiday closures observed. The showroom also hosts events such as the “On Display: Dedicated to Art” exhibition, which pairs paintings and prints with handmade wooden furniture through October 31, 2026.

The showroom serves visitors to Maine, including residential customers and design professionals seeking Thos. Moser furniture. The showroom’s primary role is to display and sell the manufacturer’s furniture rather than to produce it.
